newsitem.title: CHINA: S.Korea minister discusses four-way talks in China.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea minister discusses four-way talks in China.

text.p: Beijing on Monday told visiting South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha that China wanted to join talks for Korean peace, but Seoul and rival Pyongyang must first narrow their differences, South Korean officials said.

Yoo met his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen for four hours of discussions on bilateral issues and questions facing the tense and divided Korean peninsula, said Chang Moon-ik, spokesman of the South Korean embassy in Beijing.

China had signalled its willingness to consider participation in four-way talks that would bring together Seoul, Pyongyang, Washington and Beijing -- the main combatants in the 1950-53 Korean civil war, Chang said.
"In principle, China would like to participate in four-way talks, but there are some conditions," he said.
"There should be progress evident between South and North, then China will participate," he said.

Beijing believed the two Koreas, which are yet to agree on peace terms more than four decades after the end of the civil war, would have to be the main players in discussions aimed at ending conflict on the peninsula, he said.
"(The Chinese) stance has not changed," he said.

Beijing's involvement in the four-way talks is seen as crucial by Seoul and Washington, which proposed the negotiations as a way of ending decades of military standoff along Korea's 38th parallel that divides North and South.
While the socialist solidarity between Beijing and Pyongyang has weakened in recent years, China is still seen as enjoying some influence over its isolated and hungry Stalinist neighbour.

During their talks, Seoul's Yoo and China's Qian had also stressed the need to develop the five-year-old Sino-South Korean diplomatic relationship, and had agreed to hold working-level meetings on judicial cooperation and other issues, Chang said.
Both sides affirmed their opposition to plans by China's island arch-rival Taiwan to ship nuclear waste for dumping in cash-strapped North Korea, he said.
